---
title: "Room layout"
---

Positioning plan for 4 subwoofers and 4 error microphones, matched to the
[selected build](bom.qmd#selected-build). Dimensions below assume a nominal
$4.0 \times 3.5 \times 2.4\ \mathrm{m}$ bedroom; the placement *rules* are
dimension-independent, and exact positions get refined by the room-mode model
(workstream 2) and the level-vs-position map once measured.

![Nominal layout, top view. Generated by
[`scripts/room_layout.py`](https://github.com/madi-lts/roomANC/blob/claude/determined-ritchie-ma10cm/scripts/room_layout.py).](images/room-layout.png){#fig-layout}

## Subwoofers: four corners, floor level

Every rigid-walled room mode has a pressure antinode in every corner, so a
corner-loaded source couples to **all** modes — there is no better actuator
position, and with one sub per corner the controller holds independent
authority over the four lowest mode families. Practical points:

- Push each cabinet into its corner (10–30 cm from both walls). At
  $\lambda = c/f \approx 5.8\ \mathrm{m}$ for the 59 Hz tone, the cabinet is
  acoustically a point monopole: its facing direction is immaterial, so the
  driver can face *into* the corner — which incidentally hides the exposed
  cone from the cat.
- Set each sub's low-pass crossover to maximum (130 Hz on the selected
  unit) and leave polarity at 0°; whatever the settings, they are baked into
  the identified secondary paths $\hat{S}_{ml}$ and must never change
  afterward without re-identification (spec R7).
- Decouple cabinets from the floor with isolation pads: this is a rental
  (less vibration into the slab and the neighbors), and it keeps the
  structure-borne path from re-injecting the antinoise somewhere the
  controller can't see.

## The feedback question

"Feedback from the woofers into the error mics" covers three physically
distinct phenomena; only one of them is a real design constraint here.

**1. Reference contamination (the classic ANC feedback instability).**
In a feedforward system with a physical reference microphone, the control
loudspeakers' output leaks back into the reference sensor, closing an
unintended loop — the acoustic analogue of PA howlround, conventionally
fought with feedback-neutralization filters. **This loop does not exist in
our design**: the reference is synthesized inside the controller (a tracked
quadrature oscillator, see the
[spec](spec.qmd#tonal-structure-adaptive-notch-form)), so there is no
acoustic input for the woofers to contaminate. This is the strongest of the
several reasons the synthesized reference was chosen. (If the optional wall
accelerometer is ever used, the woofers couple to the wall and the issue
returns in structure-borne form — it would need a neutralization filter
$\hat{F}(z)$ subtracting the predicted woofer contribution from the sensor.)

**2. Error mics hearing the woofers — not a bug.** The path from each
woofer $l$ to each error mic $m$ *is* the secondary path $S_{ml}(z)$ that
FxLMS is built around; the error mics are supposed to hear the woofers,
because $e_m = d_m + \sum_l s_{ml} * y_l$ is the quantity being driven to
zero. The genuine pathology is **near-field bias**: within the reactive
(evanescent) near field of a source, $kr \lesssim 1$ — i.e.
$r \lesssim \lambda/2\pi \approx 0.93\ \mathrm{m}$ at 59 Hz, where
$k = 2\pi/\lambda$ is the wavenumber and $r$ the source–mic distance — the
pressure is dominated by the local $1/r$-divergent term rather than the
modal field. A mic parked there over-weights its nearest woofer, the
controller "wins" by nulling that one mic locally while under-cancelling
the room, and the $M \times L$ secondary-path matrix picks up one dominant
entry per row and conditions badly. **Rule: every error mic stays at least
1 m from every woofer** — the dashed exclusion circles in the figure. With
corner subs and mics in the occupied zone this is nearly automatic.

**3. Instability through secondary-path error.** FxLMS remains stable while
the phase of $\hat{S}_{ml}$ is within ±90° of the true path at the control
frequencies. Moving a mic, rotating it, bumping a sub, or large furniture
changes rotate that phase — the fix is procedural, not geometric: fixed
mounts, and re-identification after any disturbance (R7), with a small
leakage term in the weight update for robustness.

## Error microphones: positions

The adaptive loop minimizes $\sum_m e_m^2$, so the deep quiet zone forms
around the microphones, weighted by how well they observe the controlled
modes. Four rules generate the figure's positions:

1. **Put mics where your head goes.** M1/M2 flank the pillow zone at
   $h = 0.6\ \mathrm{m}$ (head height lying down), ~0.6 m apart so the pair
   spans the head's excursion; M3 covers the desk at seated ear height
   $h = 1.2\ \mathrm{m}$.
2. **Stay out of every woofer's near field** (≥ 1 m, rule 2 above).
3. **Avoid symmetry planes.** Room midplanes ($x = L_x/2$, etc.) are nodal
   for every odd-order mode — a mic there is blind to those modes. All four
   positions sit off-center in every coordinate.
4. **Break planarity and vary heights.** M4 stands apart at
   $h = 1.6\ \mathrm{m}$: four non-coplanar mics at three heights keep the
   $4 \times 4$ matrix $\hat{S}$ well-conditioned and give the vertical
   modes ($f_{001} = c/2L_z \approx 71\ \mathrm{Hz}$ nominal) an observer.

## Error microphones: mounting

The mics are Samson C02s — pencil cardioid condensers — which brings two
mounting-specific issues on top of the rental and cat constraints:

- **Structure-borne pickup.** The building vibrates at exactly the
  frequencies we care about, and a mic body rigidly coupled to floor or
  furniture reads that vibration as spurious pressure. Mount each mic in an
  elastic suspension (pencil-mic shock mount, or the stock clip padded with
  foam): a suspension resonance $f_0 \approx 8\ \mathrm{Hz}$ attenuates
  59 Hz body vibration by roughly $(f_0/f)^2 \approx -17\ \mathrm{dB}$, and
  softer is better. Prefer stands on rugs/pads over clamps on large
  resonant panels (a shaking headboard is the worst host).
- **Fixed orientation.** A cardioid responds to a pressure-gradient
  component, so its reading in a standing-wave field depends on aim.
  That is harmless — the loop minimizes what it measures, and the
  (huge) 59 Hz signal is far above the capsule's low-end rolloff — but the
  aim becomes part of the identified $\hat{S}$: set each mic pointing into
  the room interior, mark the position and rotation with tape, and re-run
  identification after any bump.
- **Rental + cat.** Nothing fastens to walls. M1/M2 ride short boom arms
  clamped to the bed frame (through foam), or weighted round-base stands
  beside the headboard; M3 clamps to the desk; M4 is a straight stand with
  a weighted base in the open. Keep capsules ≥ 1.2 m up where feasible,
  leave no dangling cable slack (coil and tie at the stand base), and run
  floor cables through split-loom or cord covers — a batted-off mic is a
  re-identification event at best (R7) and a watchdog mute at worst (R8).

## Acceptance

The layout is validated, not assumed: after installation, run the
[verification plan](spec.qmd#measurement-and-verification-plan) — if the
measured attenuation at the grid points fails R2 while the error mics read
deep nulls, that is the near-field/observability signature, and the
response is to re-spread the mics, not to raise loop gain.
